extracted.intended_audience: aspiring authors and young literary practitioners (especially those preparing periodical works)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and stylistic guidance for writers about language, terminology, and the business of publishing (particularly periodicals). Includes when to coin or revive terms, how to avoid pedantry, citation practice, and cautions about self-publishing and subscriber reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use neologisms to convey genuinely new ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: When a new sense must be conveyed, a new term both aids the recollection of the meaning and prevents its being confounded with the usual import of an existing word (illustrated by the coinage of 'esemplastic').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coin a new word when you must convey a novel concept that would be confused with existing vocabulary. A new term can help readers recall the intended meaning and avoid the double effort of redefining a familiar word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedantry = inappropriate use of words for time/place/company
rubrics_metrics.description: “Pedantry consists in the use of words unsuitable to the time, place, and company.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge diction by audience and context: scholarly technical language used in casual company is pedantic, and conversely insisting only on colloquial terms for academic discourse is also a form of pedantry. Both scholarly ostentation and vulgar pretension are objectionable in different ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer introducing new terms to reassigning old ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Using old words with new meanings demands a twofold exertion of thought (learn the new definition and unlearn the old); therefore introducing new terms (as Linnaeus or modern chemical nomenclature did) is preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reusing familiar vocabulary with altered technical senses when possible; coin or adopt a new, precise term to reduce cognitive load and ambiguity for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restore obsolete terms when justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Where it is possible to recall an inappropriately discarded term that had become obsolete, restoring it is less evil than coining anew.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an older word (with an appropriate sense) can be revived without confusion, prefer revival over neologism—this can preserve historical precision and avoid unnecessary coinage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautious discrimination of closely related terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully distinguish allied words (e.g., sensuous vs sensual vs sensitive vs sensible; reason vs understanding) to preserve nuance and avoid moral or semantic confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise in selecting terms whose connotations differ; map out the distinctions and use the word that matches the intended philosophical, ethical, or rhetorical sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reintroduce established philosophical vocabulary when concise
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like objective and subjective, or intuition used in different senses, can be re-introduced because they concisely express distinctions essential to speculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not avoid technical philosophical terms simply to appear colloquial; if an established term succinctly captures a needed distinction, reintroduce it for clarity and brevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: High ideas require symbolic expression and may involve contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: “An idea, in the highest sense of that word, cannot be conveyed but by a symbol; and, except in geometry, all symbols of necessity involve an apparent contradiction.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that some profound concepts must be expressed symbolically or paradoxically; writing intended for readers who cannot pierce such symbolic 'husk' is not aimed at them. Where full disclosure could cause harm, the writer may legitimately speak mythically or equivocally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation practice and acknowledgment of influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity of thought or phrase is not proof of borrowing; the author should warn readers that coincidence or common schooling can produce resemblance. Absence of precise references should not be taken as intentional concealment if a general acknowledgment is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge intellectual debts; where precise citation is impracticable, offer a general acknowledgment to avoid charges of plagiarism. Be transparent about limited access to sources when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on raw subscriber counts without verifying commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Subscription lists are unreliable: names may be added without authority, extorted by friends, or given provisionally with intent to drop the work later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before depending on subscription numbers, verify actual commitment (payments/firm pledges). Anecdotes (e.g., many subscribers dropping out before payment) illustrate the practical financial risk of trusting nominal lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid combining author and publisher functions; prefer trade publication or sell copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: Deviating from the ordinary trade mode of publishing adds costs and hazards; the prudent route is to sell the copy-right (or otherwise use trade publishing) rather than attempt to be both author and publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-publishing can require significant upfront costs, logistical burdens, and emotional strain; selling copyright for a moderate sum (and peace of mind) is often wiser than risking higher profit for greater anxiety. If trade practices cannot be changed, work within them rather than complain about individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that controversial or abstruse content will reduce your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Works on abstruse themes or truths that demand effort of thought and patience of attention will likely attract a scant audience; likewise, offending readers' expectations (e.g., political or religious stances) will cost subscribers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the goal is wide readership or subscriber retention, align content with audience expectations; if pursuing difficult or unpopular truths, accept that the audience will be smaller and prepare financially and temperamentally for that outcome (examples: losing many subscribers after a controversial essay).
